source: Klein et al. (2014) Investigating variation in replicability: a Many Labs replication project. Social Psychology 45(3):142-152 (Table 2, anchoring rows)
finding: Re-opened at source (PDF text). All four Jacowitz and Kahneman anchoring items replicated in every one of the 36 samples. Anchoring was the largest effect in the project and was larger than in the original.
numbers: 13 effects, 36 samples, 6,344 participants in total. Anchoring (between-subjects, one anchor then one estimate), replication d as median over samples / pooled weighted: babies born 2.43 / 2.42 (99% CI 2.33 to 2.51; t(5607)=90.49); Mt Everest 2.00 / 2.23; Chicago 1.88 / 1.79; distance to NYC 1.18 / 1.17. Share of samples with p<.05 in the expected direction = 1.00 for all four items; opposite direction = 0.00. Original aggregate d = 0.93 (95% CI .51 to 1.33). For contrast: allowed/forbidden d 1.88, gain-loss framing 0.58, sunk costs 0.32, flag priming 0.02, currency priming 0.00.
limits: The original anchoring number is a mean point-biserial correlation over 15 questions in a test-retest design, so original-to-replication d is not like for like (the paper says so). Heterogeneity across samples was also largest for anchoring (Q up to 312.75 for Chicago). Four items only. Closes gap 9 for Many Labs 1 and fixes K09 and K31 at source.
agent_relevance: Human numeric anchoring is large and stable, so a model trained on human text should show it. Strip or fence any number in the input that is not evidence.

source: Hertwig and Gigerenzer (1999) The 'conjunction fallacy' revisited. J Behavioral Decision Making 12:275-305
finding: Re-opened at source (PDF text). The Linda error in the probability-ranking format is about 83 to 88 percent. It falls to 0 to 13 percent when people give frequency estimates with 'frequency' wording. Part of the drop is response mode and part is the word.
numbers: Study 1 (Munich): 15 of 18 (83%) violated the conjunction rule; 39 paraphrases of 'probability', 18 different meanings. Study 3: 20 students, frequency estimates, 0% violations. Study 4 (Salzburg, 98 students over several conditions): 13% (3 of 23) in the frequency condition. Reviewed literature: health-survey item 58% (probability) vs 25% (frequency) in Tversky and Kahneman; Fiedler 1988 73% vs 23% (exp 1) and 70% vs 25% (exp 2); Reeves and Lockhart 59% vs 35%; Jones et al. 1995 85% vs 81% (only 4 points). Median violation 87% (17 conditions, 10 studies, probability ranking) vs 17% (frequency estimation): 70 points. Response mode alone explains about 30 points, under half.
limits: Cells are about 20 to 25 people. The frequency effect was not general: Jones et al. found almost none, which the authors explain by that study not asking for a frequency judgment. Kahneman and Tversky (1996) disputed the pragmatic reading. Closes gap 9 for this paper and replaces the Wikipedia-based a21 numbers.
agent_relevance: Wording decides how much of the bias appears. For the agent, ask for counts ('out of 100 women like Linda, how many') and ask for an estimate, not a ranking.

source: Epstein et al. (2025) LLMs are Overconfident: Evaluating Confidence Interval Calibration with FermiEval (arXiv 2510.26995)
finding: Models asked for 90, 95, 99 and 99.8 percent intervals on Fermi estimation questions cover the truth far less often than asked, and coverage barely rises as the requested level rises. This is a direct LLM test of the overprecision result.
numbers: Science Olympiad Fermi questions, 500 train and 500 test, answers 10^-100 to 10^100. Models: GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Haiku, Grok-3-mini and grok-4-fast, plus Qwen2.5-32B, OpenHermes-2.5-Mistral-7B, TinyLlama (all under-cover). GPT-4o-mini observed coverage with a plain prompt: 0.63 at nominal 0.90, 0.59 at 0.95, 0.64 at 0.99. With a log-prob heuristic: 0.85, 0.89, 0.90. Split-conformal calibration reaches near-nominal coverage and cut the Winkler score by about 25.2%, 27.8% and 59.4% at p=0.90, 0.95, 0.99.
limits: Fermi order-of-magnitude questions with exponent answers, not general-knowledge ranges as in the 1974 test. Small cost-efficient models. One prompt format. The log-prob heuristic works for GPT-4o-mini only and got worse than baseline on Winkler score at p=0.90 (27.92 to 33.32).
agent_relevance: Treat any interval a model states as too narrow: asked for 90%, real coverage was about 63% in the best-documented case. Widen by calibration; do not trust the stated level.

source: Hobor, Brcic, Kovac and Poje (2026) Bayesian Elicitation with LLMs: Model Size Helps, Extra Reasoning Doesn't Always (arXiv 2604.01896)
finding: Eleven LLMs gave 95 percent credible intervals for population statistics. All were badly overconfident and more reasoning effort did not fix it. Conformal recalibration did.
numbers: 400 questions (100 each from Big Five, NHANES, NCD-RisC, Glassdoor). Raw 95% intervals held the truth 9% to 44% of the time across all model-by-effort cells; no cell above 44%. Reasoning effort (low, medium, high) gave no consistent gain in accuracy or calibration. Against a naive 50% baseline models won: Big Five 88.9%, Glassdoor 65.7%, NCD-RisC 69.6%, NHANES 60.9%. For health, median predicted 18.0% vs true 40.3%, which the authors call a strong anchoring toward low values. Web search hurt already-accurate models (25 questions per dataset, Wilcoxon).
limits: Recall of real-world statistics, not a judgment task with an injected anchor. Preprint. The anchoring label is the authors' reading, not a tested manipulation.
agent_relevance: More thinking budget did not widen the intervals. If the agent states ranges, add an explicit widening rule or calibration step rather than more reasoning.

source: Bahaj, Rahimi, Chetouani and Ghogho (2025) Gauging Overprecision in LLMs: An Empirical Study (arXiv 2504.12098)
finding: GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4o-mini were asked for numeric intervals at 60 to 95 percent confidence. Hit rate stayed flat whatever confidence level was imposed, and interval length did not track the requested level.
numbers: 10 runs per cell. GPT-4o-mini vanilla: FinQA hit@95 21.14, hit@90 18.95, hit@60 17.04; Medical 60.31 / 60.41 / 60.39; MMLU 67.05 / 68.21 / 68.85. CoT raised GPT-4o-mini (MMLU 79.56 at 95, Medical 68.49, FinQA 21.54) but stayed far below 95. GPT-3.5-turbo hit rates 6.2 to 7.4 (FinQA), 47 to 49 (Medical), 58 to 60 (MMLU); CoT changed little and slightly hurt MMLU. Correlation of interval length with confidence level between -0.0089 and 0.0143 in every cell. Self-refinement lowered precision.
limits: Two older cheap models. Questions are numeric extractions from FinQA, MedQA, MMLU, not almanac items. Hit rate depends on answer scale. The paper cannot tell whether the cause is no concept of confidence or no instruction following.
agent_relevance: Asking for 'a 90% range' does not make the range 90%. Do not use the stated level as a number.

source: Borjigin, Hermann, Cyron and Aydin (2026) AnchorBench: A Multi-Pathway Benchmark for the Anchoring Effect in LLMs (arXiv 2608.14320, COLM 2026)
finding: First direct measurement of anchors arriving through five pathways: prompt, earlier conversation turn, demonstrations, retrieved text, tool output. Conversation-history and tool anchors move answers substantially; anchors in demonstrations barely do. Frontier models ignore irrelevant numbers but still move toward plausible ones.
numbers: 14 models (10 open-weight, 4 frontier, labelled 5.4-mini, Haiku 4.5, 2.5-Flash, 3-mini), greedy decoding, 360 items per suite. Mean anchor influence index (UAI; 0 none, 1 full move to the anchor), irrelevant / plausible: External 0.05 / 0.22; History 0.05 / 0.34; ICL metadata 0.02 / 0.03; RAG 0.03 / 0.13; Tool 0.07 / 0.18; all pathways 0.04 / 0.18. Frontier rows of Table 1: irrelevant anchor -0.02 to 0.10 (mostly 0.00 to 0.03); plausible anchor External 0.07 to 0.16, Tool 0.01 to 0.06, History -0.06 to 0.10. Plausible anchors raised mean error by +3.6 points (External) and +3.5 (Tool). Error-increasing shifts 29% vs error-reducing 23% overall (37% vs 20% for plausible anchors). Even models above 95% control accuracy stay susceptible to plausible anchors.
limits: History compares a two-stage protocol with a single-stage control, so its size is inflated (matched analysis cuts the gap by up to 70% for some models). Tool format differs by model family. The History anchor is the model's own earlier answer, which is the case our agent meets most. No fresh-context condition was run. A plausible numeric anchor can be rational evidence, so not all of the shift is bias.
agent_relevance: Closest direct data for gap 6: an earlier guess or tool number in context moves later estimates about a third of the way to it on average, and strong models are mostly safe from irrelevant numbers but not from plausible ones. Keep earlier guesses out of the context that produces the next estimate, or pass them as labelled evidence.

source: Borjigin et al. (2026) AnchorBench, Appendix A.16 mitigation headroom probe (arXiv 2608.14320)
finding: Three cheap prompt fixes were tried on two 7-8B models: an 'ignore' instruction, a self-check turn, and a CoT that lists evidence first. 'Ignore' reduced anchor discrimination in all four cells. Self-check raised it for one model. CoT helped one model a lot and the other not at all.
numbers: Disc = plausible minus irrelevant influence. External: Qwen-7B baseline 0.26, ignore 0.16, self-check 0.45, CoT 0.14; Llama-8B baseline 0.30, ignore 0.10, self-check 0.28, CoT 0.31. RAG: Qwen-7B 0.20 / 0.14 / 0.30 / 0.03; Llama-8B 0.16 / 0.04 / 0.11 / 0.08. Control error (MAE) External: Qwen-7B 7.7 baseline, 5.0 ignore, 8.8 self-check, 1.1 CoT. Ignore mean reduction -0.12 across the four cells.
limits: Two small models, two suites, one run each at temperature 0, tokens not reported (CoT and self-check cost more than 'ignore'). The 'ignore' line was about irrelevant numbers and may also suppress useful plausible anchors. The authors say mitigations weaken but do not remove anchoring.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 8: a short 'use only the task evidence' line gave a steady gain at almost no tokens; a self-check turn can raise anchoring. This sits against a28 and b14 where 'ignore the hint' failed on GPT-4 class models with expert anchors.

source: Anchoring Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge Systems: Prior Scores Compromise Evaluation Independence (arXiv 2608.25869)
finding: A prior score placed in context as metadata pulls later scores toward it in seven of eight models, including Claude-4.5-Sonnet and GPT-4.1. A chain-of-thought instruction made it worse and an explicit warning did not shrink the total shift.
numbers: 8 models, 20 fixed texts, 100 calls per model-task-temperature-condition cell, 4 temperatures, 185,271 valid of 192,000 calls. Prior score drawn uniformly from [0, 3.99) against an accept threshold of 4.0. Shift (anchored minus no-metadata): Llama-3.2-3B -0.254 (d -0.71), GPT-4.1 -0.411 (d -0.67), Qwen2.5-7B -0.233 (d -0.51), Claude-4.5-Sonnet -0.706 (d -0.44; acceptance rate -22.29 points), DeepSeek-R1 -0.269 (d -0.25), Gemma-2-9B -0.072, Llama-3.3-70B -0.025, Llama-3.1-8B -0.009 (CI includes 0). GPT-4.1, one summarisation pair, T=0: baseline shift -0.429, with CoT -0.633, with explicit warning -0.457; the warning removed the within-condition slope (0.2674 to -0.0066) but not the total shift.
limits: Read through a fetch summary of the paper text, not as a raw PDF. Prior scores were always below the threshold, so part of the shift may be rational. Mitigations were tested on one item pair for one model. No fresh-context condition: the paper says removing the prior is the direct fix but gives no effect size.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 evidence: earlier scores in context anchor judges. If the agent scores several items in one context, score each in a fresh context or hide earlier scores. CoT is not a safe fix.

source: Huang et al. (2025/2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data (SynAnchors), mitigation section (arXiv 2505.15392)
finding: Re-read for the mitigation table. No conventional fix removes anchoring. The best fix, writing your own criteria first, cut the anchored share by about 10 points on one model and not on the other.
numbers: 100 questions (60 semantic, 40 numerical), 11 models. Total anchored share: Qwen2.5-0.5B 60.5%, Llama-3.2-1B 57.1%, GPT-4o-mini 37.0%, GPT-4o 27.3%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%, Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%. Mitigation on Llama-3.1-8B / Qwen2.5-7B, baseline 34.7% / 40.0%: 'think carefully' prompt 36.8% / 43.0%; knowledge enhancement 50.5% / 40.0%; self-improving (reflection turn) 38.4% / 48.0%; LoRA adversarial fine-tune 33.3% / 37.0%; DoLa decoding 37.5-38.5% / 38.0-40.0%; Anti-DP (set your own criteria, then answer) 24.7% / 40.8%. Causal tracing on Llama-3.1-8B (10 questions): anchor tokens matter in early layers and fade higher up.
limits: Read through a fetch summary. Mitigations only on two 7-8B models. Plain CoT and an explicit 'ignore the anchor' line were not in the list. Some Qwen3 cells had 30 samples instead of 100. Anti-DP lowered semantic anchoring on Qwen (0.463 to 0.344) but raised numeric anchoring (0.233 to 0.315).
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 8: late prompt fixes that talk about the anchor ('think carefully', reflect) did not help or made it worse; forming own criteria first helped one model. Supports removing the number rather than arguing with it.

source: Takenami, Huang, Murawaki and Chu (2025) How Does Cognitive Bias Affect LLMs? Anchoring in Price Negotiation Simulations (EMNLP Findings; arXiv 2508.21137), Tables 2 and 4
finding: Telling the buyer model that the seller will use an anchoring tactic recovers only part of the loss. A reasoning model as buyer recovers more, and QwQ recovered all of it when informed. This is the closest LLM analogue to knowing the direction of the bias.
numbers: Buyer utility, baseline / seller anchors / seller anchors and buyer informed: GPT-4o -0.04 / -0.41 / -0.35; GPT-4 0.20 / -0.34 / -0.21; Llama 3 0.42 / -0.21 / -0.02; Qwen2.5 0.02 / -0.39 / -0.19. Loss from baseline, anchored / anchored and informed: GPT-4o 0.38 / 0.32; o1 0.40 / 0.20; Qwen2.5 0.41 / 0.20; QwQ 0.26 / 0.00 (o1 and QwQ informed-condition gains significant by paired t-test). In 35 of 50 matched cases o1 agreed a lower price than GPT-4o when informed. All pairwise condition differences significant; 322 simulations.
limits: Being told 'the seller uses anchoring' names the tactic, not the direction of the model's own error. The direction (a high opening offer) is obvious here, so this tests awareness more than direction knowledge. One scenario family. No accuracy-instruction arm, so gap 10 stays open as a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Naming the likely bias source helps a little for plain models and more for reasoning models. An S1 note such as 'this figure came from the counterparty or an earlier guess, so it likely pulls estimates up' is cheap to test.

source: Yax, Anllo and Palminteri (2023/2024) Studying and improving reasoning in humans and machines (arXiv 2309.12485), new Linda/Bill vignettes
finding: Checked contamination directly. GPT-3 models found the original Linda text unusually familiar (log-probability curve), so the authors wrote 1024 new Linda/Bill vignettes with new names, items and domains. On the new items GPT-3 was near chance, ChatGPT beat humans, and GPT-4 was almost perfect. So GPT-4's success on Linda is not only memory of the famous text.
numbers: 2048 vignettes (512 Linda, 512 Bill, both option orders); 128 human and 128 model 'participants' each solved 8 Linda and 8 Bill items. GPT-3 family: Bill 0.53, Linda 0.46 mean accuracy (Linda lower, P<.0001). Humans: Bill 0.83, Linda 0.56 (gap 0.27). ChatGPT: Linda 0.70 (0.14 above humans), gap 0.12. GPT-4: Bill 0.99, Linda 0.98. Plain joint-probability arithmetic: humans 0.34 vs davinci-003 0.96. For davinci-003 a step-by-step prompt raised accuracy by 0.32 (Bill) and 0.39 (Linda); it did nothing for humans. Strong effect of answer-option order in models, none in humans.
limits: 2023 models only (GPT-3 family, ChatGPT, GPT-4); no 2025 to 2026 model. Two-option forced choice. Human participants were online workers who wrote short answers, which may understate their ability. Closes part of gap 3 for conjunction items at GPT-4 level; the 2025 to 2026 part is still open.
agent_relevance: Perturbed vignettes were still solved by a strong model, so success there is not only contamination for conjunction items. But option order mattered, so randomise option order in any check.

source: PsyAgentBench: Recognition, Simulation, and Refusal, a contamination-aware study (arXiv 2609.22090)
finding: Classic social-psychology paradigms were run on LLM agents with textbook wording and with structurally matched counterfactual content. Effects that looked human often depended on the paradigm being named, and anchoring behaved unlike humans: zero on real facts, near total on invented quantities.
numbers: 41,904 logged trials, 20 seeds per cell. Anchoring index for gpt-oss-120B (human about 0.49): 0.000 in canonical cells and 0.90 to 1.01 in counterfactual cells (invented quantities). Framing effect (human about 0.50): 0.619 canonical, 0.787 counterfactual. Sunk cost 0.000 in most cells (human about 0.35). Asch conformity for gpt-oss-120B 83.3% canonical vs 39.2% counterfactual; Llama 3.3 70B 46.2% vs 3.8% (sign of textbook recall). Linda was not tested.
limits: Read through a fetch summary. Mostly one model (gpt-oss-120B); only Asch used three models. One fixed scenario per domain, no mixed-effects tests. The authors note that following an invented anchor may be rational because it is the only signal.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a model anchors hard when it has no prior of its own and not at all when it knows the fact. So anchor risk is largest on numbers the agent cannot check, which is where tool outputs and earlier guesses sit.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing (SACD) for LLMs in decision-making (arXiv 2504.04141), tables and setup
finding: Re-opened tables. SACD gave the lowest bias scores, but the bias was injected into the prompt as a stated statistic (for example 'among all the questions, 70% have the answer B'), and SACD was allowed up to three rounds of three calls each. Cost was not matched.
numbers: 500 samples per setting (100 for GPT-4o) in finance (FOMC), health (PubMedQA) and legal (LegalBench); T=0; max 3 iterations with early stop. FOMC Llama-3.1-8B average bias score: vanilla 0.3805, CoT 0.3425, zero-shot debiasing 0.2965, self-help 0.2100, SACD 0.1570; anchoring column: vanilla 0.4060, CoT 0.4120, self-help 0.1740, SACD 0.1460. Second table Llama-3.1-8B average: vanilla 0.5570, CoT 0.4215, self-help 0.2625, SACD 0.1235. Llama-3.1-70B FOMC: vanilla 0.1648, CoT 0.2220, self-help 0.1885; SACD round 1 0.2070 (worse than vanilla), rounds 2 and 3 0.1460 and 0.1175. Few-shot prompting raised bias on 70B (0.3655). Error analysis, finance: 257/500 errors for self-help vs 61/500 for SACD.
limits: The biases are inserted cues in decision tasks (the anchor is a stated class proportion), not original Tversky and Kahneman tasks, and the score is how often the model follows the cue. No accuracy-at-equal-tokens result. Round 1 can be worse than doing nothing on a strong model. Gap 5 closes only in part: SACD wins on its own benchmark at a cost of 3 to 9 extra calls.
agent_relevance: Detect-and-rewrite works when the bias is a visible cue in the prompt. It is an input rewrite (strip the cue), which fits S1 input hygiene, but it must be budgeted: round 1 alone can hurt.

source: Araya (2025) Do Chains-of-Thoughts of LLMs Suffer from Hallucinations, Cognitive Biases, or Phobias in Bayesian Reasoning? (arXiv 2503.15268), results table
finding: One Bayesian puzzle and a handful of runs on three reasoning models. Models did not spontaneously use natural frequencies. When told to, they got the right answer in all 3 runs per prompt, but the reasoning was often flawed. A case study, not a test of the frequency-format effect.
numbers: One lie-detection colouring-book problem (answer: book 3). Models Gemini Flash 2.0, o3-mini, DeepSeek R1. No strategy named: 2 of 4 runs correct and 0 of 3 models used natural frequencies. Prompts naming natural frequencies, whole objects or coloured blocks: 3 of 3 correct each, but Gemini's reasoning was judged flawed in all three and DeepSeek computed 50% in the frequency run.
limits: One to two runs per cell. No probability-format control with the same prompt. Gap 4 stays open: no study was found that measures accuracy on conjunction or Bayes items in counts format vs probability format for a current model across arithmetic difficulty.
agent_relevance: A counts rewrite should be done by the scaffold, not requested of the model: left alone, reasoning models stay symbolic.

source: Harshavardhan (2026) Self-Anchoring Calibration Drift in LLMs: How Multi-Turn Conversations Reshape Model Confidence (arXiv 2603.01239)
finding: Models building on their own earlier answers over five turns changed their expressed confidence, in model-specific ways. The control that asked the same questions independently behaved differently from the self-anchoring condition. Effects were near zero on factual items and largest on open-ended ones.
numbers: 150 questions; the self-anchoring condition used n=15 questions per model. Claude Sonnet 4.6 mean confidence drift -0.032 (t(14)=-2.43, p=.029, d=-0.63) and calibration error drift F(4,56)=22.77, eta-squared .791. GPT-5.2 +0.026 in open-ended domains. Gemini 3.1 Pro no drift (t(14)=0.38, p=.710), but in the independent-repetition control its calibration error fell from .327 to near zero while self-anchoring kept it flat at .333.
limits: Abstract and design read; very small n per model; the pre-registered hypotheses were only partly confirmed; this measures confidence, not numeric anchoring. Temperature 0.7, fresh API call per trial.
agent_relevance: Gap 6, weak support: re-asking the same item in a fresh context can improve calibration where building on the earlier turn does not. Fresh context per estimate is cheap to test.

source: Weerasekara, Kamarthi and Isaacs (2026) Conditional Cognitive Biases in LLMs: How Biased User Turns Modulate In-Context Reasoning (arXiv 2608.05166)
finding: A 9 by 9 design (nine biases in the model's task, nine in an earlier user turn) over eight models. Merely adding any earlier user turn raised bias in seven of eight models, while the biased content of that turn mostly lowered it. Anchoring and confirmation were insensitive to the content of the user turn.
numbers: 8 models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Haiku, Llama-3.1-70B and 8B, Qwen-2.5-72B, Phi-4, Gemma-2-9B, DeepSeek-V3), T=0. Presence effect: Llama-3.1-8B +0.086, Llama-3.1-70B +0.061, Gemma +0.058, Phi-4 +0.052, Qwen +0.046, DeepSeek-V3 +0.025, GPT-4o +0.019, Claude-3.5-Haiku -0.101. Content effect negative in most models (for example Llama-3.1-70B -0.039). Same-bias contagion: no diagonal advantage (Llama-3.1-8B p=0.79).
limits: Read through a fetch summary; the last 9,455 characters were not read. Bias scoring is the authors' own. No mitigation condition. The user-turn bias is stated in words, not a number anchor.
agent_relevance: Prior context adds a general push toward bias even when its content is neutral. Another reason to keep the estimating context short.

source: Liu, Chen and Zhong (2025) Large Language Newsvendor: Decision Biases and Cognitive Mechanisms (arXiv 2512.12552)
finding: In a repeated newsvendor task the first scenario shapes later orders: GPT-4 kept adjusting in the same direction after the margin condition flipped. Biases stayed even when the optimal formula was given.
numbers: GPT-4, GPT-4o, LLaMA-8B; 15 rounds. GPT-4 deviated up to 70% more than human benchmarks. When GPT-4 saw the high-margin scenario first, 'toward demand' adjustments were 77.5% in the first four rounds and 80.0% right after the switch to low margin; the reverse order showed a similar persistence. GPT-4o was near optimal.
limits: Operations task with its own theory; the 'paradox of intelligence' reading and the mechanism names are the authors'. Number of repeated runs not checked. Order effect shown by adjustment-direction shares, not an effect size.
agent_relevance: Weak support for gap 6: early rounds set a frame that persists across later items in one context.

source: Owusu and Feldman (2026) Anchoring Depends on Confidence and Post-Training in Language Models (ACL 2026 short, abstract page)
finding: Abstract only. Base, instruction-tuned and distilled Llama and Qwen models were primed with irrelevant numbers. Anchoring susceptibility falls as model confidence rises, whether or not the confident answer is right. High anchors pull harder than low anchors.
numbers: No effect sizes on the page. Tested: base, instruction-tuned and distilled variants of Llama and Qwen.
limits: Only the abstract was read (the fetch could not open the PDF). Open-weight models. Cannot say how it bears on a late prompt instruction.
agent_relevance: Gap 8, indirect: the anchor matters most where the model is unsure. This predicts an accuracy instruction will not help on items where the model has no strong prior; consistent with d12.

source: Wu, Guo and Yiu (2026) Bias by Necessity: Impossibility Theorems for Sequential Processing (arXiv 2605.08716)
finding: A theory paper that predicts the anchor effect depends on anchor position in the context and reports 12 model results plus two human experiments. Low weight: single group, theory-driven, mostly older named models.
numbers: Table 3 anchoring rates: GPT-4 42.3%, Claude-3 38.7%, Gemini-1.5 44.1%, Llama-3-70B 51.2%, Mistral-Large 38.4%, Command-R+ 47.8%. 200 anchoring trials per model, 20 Jacowitz-Kahneman items, anchor placed at one of 8 sentence positions. Human Study 1 (N=464 across both pre-registered studies): anchor-position effect d=0.52, BF10=847.
limits: The model list includes GPT-3.5, Claude-2, Gemini-1.0 and other old models labelled frontier. The exponential-decay fit (R2=0.89) was not checked against raw per-position values. The impossibility claims rest on a model, not on tests of mitigations. Not used to change any claim status.
agent_relevance: If true, an anchor early in the context has more pull than one late. Not enough to design on.

source: Chergui et al. (2026) Mitigating Anchoring Bias in LLM-Based Agents for Energy-Efficient 6G Autonomous Networks (arXiv 2606.18272)
finding: A multi-agent resource negotiation in a simulated 6G network. A 1B model clung to its first heuristic proposal and over-provisioned. Replacing the fixed first proposal with a randomised one led to more search and up to 25 percent energy saving.
numbers: Locally hosted 1B model; 0.95 s mean latency; energy saving up to 25% against a fixed-anchor baseline.
limits: Read from the PDF text (abstract and results); a 1B model in an engineering simulation; the anchor is the agent's own initial proposal; no human comparison and no control for simply exploring more. Low weight.
agent_relevance: A direct agent-style case of the first guess being sticky. Randomise or rotate the first guess when seeding a search.

source: Probabilistic Reasoning in Generative Large Language Models (arXiv 2402.09614)
finding: Percent-format probability questions and Bayesian-network queries, with tools. No natural-frequency format and no base-rate-neglect word problems, so it does not answer gap 4. It shows that code or simulation beats plain answers and plain CoT on probability questions.
numbers: Average accuracy (V2 to 10, zero-shot) GPT-3.5 / Llama3-70B / GPT-4: basic QA 7 / 8 / 18; CoT 9 / 21 / 32; PAL 19 / 40 / 54; Monte Carlo 46 / 87 / 86; ProbLog 62 / 89 / 97. Adapted CLADDER: GPT-4 20% basic, 97% ProbLog.
limits: Read through a fetch summary (first 100,000 characters). Synthetic probability puzzles in percent format, not human heuristics tasks. Authors not verified.
agent_relevance: For Bayes items the large gain comes from computation by tool or code, not from wording: do the arithmetic outside the model.
